note: A GATE THAT RECORDS ITSELF CAN BLOCK RECOVERY FROM ITS OWN FAILURE. Hit during The Confidant, and it only shows up once something else has already gone wrong, which is the worst time to meet it. SHAPE: make gate-commit appends a bookkeeping row to docs/timings.md as it runs. If the gate then FAILS, the commit is rejected but the row is already written, so the working tree is dirty in a tracked file. If you were mid-merge, git merge --abort now REFUSES: it reports Entry docs/timings.md not uptodate, cannot merge, and fatal could not reset index file to revision HEAD. The instrument that recorded the failed attempt is what stands between you and undoing it. THE FIX IS ONE LINE and worth knowing before you need it: git checkout HEAD -- docs/timings.md, then abort. The row is bookkeeping from a run that failed, so discarding it loses nothing — but you have to realise that is what is blocking you, and the error message names the file without explaining why it is dirty. WHY THIS IS A DESIGN HAZARD RATHER THAN A MISTAKE: the recording is unconditional and the failure is not, so the two are coupled in exactly the case where you least want coupling. Same family as timed.sh recording no exit code, which means a red run and a green run leave indistinguishable rows. SECOND, SEPARATE SCAR FROM THE SAME EPISODE, because it produced the dirty tree in the first place: do not chain a state-changing git command after one that can fail. I ran git commit followed by git stash apply on one line. The commit was rejected by the hook, the stash apply ran anyway, and it re-conflicted a generated file AND staged source into a pending merge where it must never be. The generalisation is not just that the second command cannot see the first failed — it is that choosing between and-and and semicolon is a failure-semantics decision made by muscle memory while typing. Rule worth adopting: any command that mutates git state gets its own invocation, and reads the previous exit code deliberately if it depends on it.
